text: This is a story about ownership that refuses to resolve its central question -- can you own what is beneath your feet? -- and is stronger for the refusal. The narrator's guilt is not offered as redemption narrative. She does not forgive herself. She does not ask to be forgiven. She presents the mathematics of her betrayal (forty dollars sent to cover a funeral, less than one-eighth of what she received for the mineral rights) and lets the numbers do their moral work. What I find most remarkable is the treatment of Nola, whom the narrator loves and cannot understand. 'I sat across from her at the kitchen table every morning for twenty-seven years... And I cannot tell you who she was.' That admission costs the narrator something real. The foxfire -- the house glowing from its own decomposition -- is the kind of image that reorganizes how you think about memory and inheritance long after you finish reading.
